candidate.blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort — Related Activity Statements, printed p.11 / PDF p.15: perform skin assessment and implement measures to maintain skin/tissue integrity; assist client with positioning and mobility; provide nonpharmacological comfort measures
candidate.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — positioning / skin and tissue integrity
candidate.educational_objective: Use lifting/repositioning techniques such as a draw sheet to minimize friction and shear and protect skin integrity.

options.A: To minimize friction and shear that can damage skin and contribute to pressure injury
options.B: To eliminate the need for skin assessment after repositioning
options.C: To increase friction so the client stays in the new position
options.D: To prevent infection by creating a sterile surface under the client

candidate.rationale: Current NCBI Nursing Fundamentals identifies friction and shear as significant risk factors for pressure injury and recommends using a draw sheet with appropriate assistance when moving a client up in bed to minimize those forces. Therefore A is correct. A draw sheet does not eliminate skin assessment, increase friction intentionally, or create a sterile surface.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Using a draw sheet during repositioning helps minimize friction and shear forces that contribute to skin/tissue damage and pressure injury.
candidate.source_locator: Pressure Injuries → Friction/Shear and Selected Interventions to Prevent/Treat Impaired Skin Integrity: friction and shear are significant pressure-injury risks; use a minimum of two-person assistance and a draw sheet to pull a client up in bed to minimize shear and friction
candidate.source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
candidate.stem: Why should the nurse use a draw sheet rather than drag a client across the bed when repositioning?
